To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Basque Arc consists, from west to east, of three thrust slices (Basque, Cantabrian and Asturian) and one thrust duplex (Santander) that are detached from their basement and cover by evaporites and associated Upper Triassic sediments; (2) these thrust slices are separated by normal faults reactivated during the Alpine orogeny, which can be related to basement discontinuity zones generated during the Hercy­nian orogeny; and

(1) the Basque Arc is an imbricated pile of tectonic slices, (2) the slices are detached by Upper Triassic evaporites and associated strata, (3) the slice-bounding thrust faults are reactivated Hercynian normal faults and, (4) the slices expose basement rocks and cover strata that were deposited on the basement after the Hercynian event.
the Basque Arc is a tectonic wedge, detached from the Hercynian basement by evaporites and associated sediments, that is bounded by normal faults reactivated during Meso-Ceno-zoic times.

the geologic evolution of the Basque–Cantabria region in the central Pyrenean–Iberian orogenic system.
the geology of an area that is not only of local interest, but also has a wider significance in the context of the geology of the Pyrenees.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Basque Arc is a tectonic window that exposes basement slices of the Hercynian Iberian Massif, and that it was not formed by a major orogeny.
the Basque Arc is a tectonic window of the Hercynian basement and its Meso-Cenzoic sedimentary cover, detached from the surrounding Pyrenean–Iberian orogenic wedge.

the Basque Arc consists in a series of thrust slices of basement rocks, with their sedimentary cover, which are detached by evaporitic rocks and associated rocks, and which have been emplaced over the Iberian Massif and the Cantabrian Arc, in a tectonic process which is still not completely understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Basque Arc consists in a set of thrust slices that have been detached from a common basement and that have moved towards the Atlantic, in the direction of the Iberian plate motion, since the Late Triassic.
the Basque Arc is not a “folded arc” but a “faulted arc”, and its basement and its sedimentary cover are not “folds and thrusts” but “detached slices” (i.e. “thrust sheets” or “nappes”).
the tectonic evolution of the Basque-Arc has been dominated by the Hercynian basement structure, which has controlled the geometry and kinematics of the Alpine thrusts.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Basque Arc has been formed as a consequence of the reactivation of the basement discontinuities during the Alpine orogeny, in response to a complex interaction between the Pyrenean and Iberian orogenic systems.
the Basque Arc is a large, complex and heterogeneous tectonic entity, with a complex and variable tectonic and stratigraphic evolution.
the tectonics of the Basque Cantabrian Basin is much more complex than previously thought.
